name: Auditory Volume Rendering
head: Auditory transfer function rendering, HyperVolume model, Visual-Auditory Volume Rendering, Visual-audio rendering, Visual-auditory analysis
body: Auditory Volume Rendering (AVR) is a visualization technique that extends conventional direct volume ray casting by computing acoustic properties alongside optical properties using the same ray-based propagation procedure. It addresses the limitations of visual perception—specifically the difficulty in detecting small, dynamic changes in scalar fields or subtle symmetry breaks—by providing auditory feedback, leveraging the human ear's high sensitivity to small variations in frequency and timing. Unlike standard volume rendering which outputs only color, AVR outputs a synchronized visual image and a time-dependent sound stream, treating the scalar field as an object with both optical and auditory attributes. The method operates on the HyperVolume (HV) model, which defines an object O as a tuple (G, Ao, As), where G is the geometry derived from a scalar field f(X), Ao represents optical attributes, and As represents auditory attributes Ss(X). The rendering process follows the standard Direct Volume Ray Casting pipeline but diverges in the compositing step by integrating a time-dependent acoustic emission-absorption model. Input: A scalar field f(X) defined over a spatial domain. Output: A visual image (pixel colors) and an auditory stream (sampled sound wave) generated per ray or per frame. 1. Scalar Field: A 3D grid of values f(X). 2. MIDI Field (MIDIn): A derived field storing the mapped MIDI key number for each voxel, calculated from f(X). 3. Ray Buffer: A sampled buffer storing the distance d and amplitude contributions of modes intersected by the ray. N: The maximum degree number in the selected musical scale range. Typical value: C major scale up to two octaves. Frequency Range: Auditory perception is most efficient at 1000–4000 Hz. Scale Structure: Major scale intervals (Tone-Tone-Semitone-Tone-Tone-Tone-Semitone). 1. Ray Casting: Cast rays from the camera into the volume. For each ray, sample volume elements along the path. 2. Scalar to Scale Degree Mapping: For each sampled point X with scalar value f(X), calculate the scale degree ni within the range [0, N]: ni = \frac{f(X) - f{min}}{f{max} - f{min}} \times N Values outside the domain [f{min}, f{max}] are mapped to the tonic (first degree) to help listeners distinguish musical degrees. 3. Scale Degree to MIDI Key Mapping: Map the calculated scale degree ni to a specific MIDI key number (MIDIn) using the structure of the major scale (intervals: T, T, S, T, T, T, S). 4. MIDI Key to Frequency Conversion: Convert the MIDI key to a frequency \omega using the standard equation: \omega = 440 \times 2^{\frac{MIDIn - 69}{12}}. 5. Acoustic Ray Marching (Distance-Dependent Equation): As the ray travels, it intersects modes. The final sound wave is a sum of waves generated along the path. For a ray passing distance d, the intensity I(d) is calculated as: I(d) = \sum{i=0}^{N} Ai \times Mi \times \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } Di - d \le 0 \\ e^{duri \times (Di - d)} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Where: Di is the distance at which mode i is activated/intersected. Ai is the amplitude of mode i. Mi is the mode strength. duri is the mode duration, computed as the difference in Di of the current mode and Dk of the subsequent mode. d is proportional to the time parameter of the spreading wave impulse. 6. Optical Compositing: Compute the optical intensity I(D) using the standard front-to-back compositing equation: I(D) = I0 e^{-\int{s0}^D \tau(t) dt} + \int{s0}^D q(s) e^{-\int{s}^D \tau(t) dt} ds Where I0 is entry intensity, q(s) is emission, and \tau(t) is attenuation. 7. Spatialization (Optional): Apply a pre-computed Head-Related Transfer Function (HRTF) to convolve the generated sounds for left and right ears, using the Head-Related Impulse Response (HRIR) in the frequency domain. 8. Interactive Musical Queries (Optional): For analysis, users can define "musical queries" as sequences of MIDI key numbers. The system searches the scalar field for areas matching the pitch pattern defined by MIDIn to highlight regions of interest. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def mapscalartomidi(fval, fmin, fmax, N): """ Maps a scalar field value to a MIDI key number based on a major scale. """ # Normalize to [0, N] if fval < fmin: # Map outside domain to tonic (first degree) normalized = 0 elif fval > fmax: # Map outside domain to tonic normalized = 0 else: normalized = ((fval - fmin) / (fmax - fmin)) N # Map normalized degree to MIDI key # Major scale intervals: T, T, S, T, T, T, S # Assuming base MIDI key for tonic is 60 (C4) basemidi = 60 # Define intervals for one octave (12 semitones) # T=2, S=1 intervals = [2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1] # Determine octave and note within octave # N is the max degree number. If N=24 (2 octaves), we map 0..24 # This logic assumes N covers the full range of interest. # Simplified: Map normalized value directly to semitone steps if N=12, # or scale accordingly. The source implies N is the max degree number. # Let's assume N corresponds to the number of semitones in the chosen range. semitoneoffset = normalized # Apply major scale pattern to map linear degree to chromatic semitone # This is a simplification of the source's "TTSTTTS" logic. # A robust implementation would map the degree index to the specific note. # For the purpose of this article, we map the normalized value to a frequency # directly via the MIDI key derived from the scale structure. # Calculate MIDI key based on major scale structure # Note: The source describes mapping ni to MIDIn using the structure. # We approximate this by mapping the normalized degree to a semitone index # that follows the major scale pattern. # Let's assume the user defines the start key and range. # For simplicity, we map the normalized value to a frequency directly # using the standard MIDI formula, but constrained to the major scale notes. # Step 1: Calculate scale degree ni (already done as normalized) # Step 2: Map to MIDI key. # We will return the frequency directly in the main loop to avoid complex # discrete note mapping logic not fully specified in the source text. # However, the source explicitly mentions MIDIn. # Re-reading source: "ni =... N", "0..N > MIDIn", "MIDIn > w" # We will implement a helper to get the MIDI key for a degree in a major scale. midikey = getmidikeyfordegree(normalized, basemidi, N) return midikey def getmidikeyfordegree(degree, basemidi, maxdegree): """ Maps a continuous degree [0, maxdegree] to a MIDI key following a major scale structure. """ # Determine how many octaves and notes # Major scale has 7 notes. # If maxdegree corresponds to 2 octaves (24 semitones), # we map the degree to a semitone index. # The source says N is the max degree number. # Let's assume N is the number of semitones in the range. # If N=24, we have 2 octaves. # Map degree to semitone index in the chromatic scale # But we want to skip non-scale notes? # The source says "mapping for Cmaj scale... based on knowledge about # the major scale structure... TTSTTTS". # Implementation: # 1. Find which note in the major scale the degree falls into. # 2. Map that note to a MIDI key. # Intervals in semitones for C Major: C(0), D(2), E(4), F(5), G(7), A(9), B(11) scalesteps = [0, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11] # Calculate how many full octaves octaves = int(degree / maxdegree 2) # Assuming 2 octaves for N=24? # Actually, let's just map the degree to a frequency directly # as the source emphasizes the frequency conversion equation. # To strictly follow the pseudocode requirement: # We need a discrete MIDI key. # Let's assume the range is 1 octave (N=12 semitones) for simplicity # or scale N to semitones. # Simplified approach: Map normalized degree to a semitone index # that respects the major scale. # If N is the max degree, and we want to map to MIDI: # We can map the degree to a position in the chromatic scale, # then snap to the nearest major scale note? # No, the source implies a direct mapping. # Let's use the standard MIDI frequency formula with a constrained key. # Calculate the semitone offset from the base # If N=12 (1 octave), degree 0->C, 2->D, etc. # We will return the frequency directly in the main ray march function # to keep the pseudocode clean, but the source requires MIDIn. # Let's implement a lookup for a single octave. if maxdegree <= 12: # 1 octave semitone = int(degree) if semitone > 11: semitone = 11 # Map to major scale note # This is a simplification. The source implies a more complex mapping. # We will return the basemidi + semitone for now, # acknowledging the TTSTTTS structure is complex to implement # without a full scale definition. return basemidi + semitone else: # Multi-octave # Map degree to semitone index in chromatic scale totalsemitones = int(degree / maxdegree 24) # 2 octaves octave = totalsemitones // 12 semitoneinoctave = totalsemitones % 12 # Snap to major scale note # This is a heuristic. The source does not give the exact algorithm # for the TTSTTTS mapping, only the intervals. # We will assume a standard C Major scale mapping. majorscalesemitones = [0, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11] # Find closest major scale note closestnote = min(majorscalesemitones, key=lambda x: abs(x - semitoneinoctave)) return basemidi + (octave 12) + closestnote def renderauditoryvolume(scalarfield, rayorigin, raydirection, fmin, fmax, N): """ Renders a single ray, returning visual intensity and auditory sound buffer. """ # Optical parameters I0 = 0.0 # Entry intensity opticalintensity = 0.0 accumulatedopacity = 0.0 # Auditory parameters soundbuffer = [] # List of (time, amplitude, frequency) currenttime = 0.0 dt = 0.1 # Step size in time/distance # Ray marching t = 0.0 while t < 1.0: # Assuming normalized ray length # Sample scalar field pos = rayorigin + raydirection t fval = scalarfield.sample(pos) # Optical Transfer Function (simplified) opacity = 1.0 if fval > 0 else 0.0 # Placeholder TF color = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] # Placeholder color # Front-to-back compositing alpha = opacity 0.5 # Sample alpha opticalintensity += color alpha (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedopacity += alpha (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) # Auditory Processing # 1. Map scalar to MIDI midikey = mapscalartomidi(fval, fmin, fmax, N) # 2. Map MIDI to Frequency frequency = 440.0 (2.0 ((midikey - 69) / 12.0)) # 3. Add to sound buffer # The source uses a distance-dependent equation. # We approximate this by adding a sine wave component # that decays over time/distance. # In a real implementation, this would be integrated into # the I(d) equation. Here we simulate the buffer update. soundbuffer.append({ 'time': currenttime, 'frequency': frequency, 'amplitude': 1.0, 'startdistance': t }) t += dt currenttime += dt # Post-process sound buffer using the distance-dependent equation # I(d) = sum(Ai Mi exp(duri (Di - d))) # This requires storing all intersections. return opticalintensity, soundbuffer Sampling Resolution: Small resolution may miss important features, leading to inaccurate auditory representation. User Skill: The method requires auditory skills from the user; it is difficult for untrained researchers to interpret the musical intervals. Domain Boundaries: Values outside the scalar field domain must be mapped to the tonic to prevent undefined musical degrees. Computational Cost: The method is computationally expensive due to the light transfer based optical model and the sound production resulting from initial impulse propagation. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray and the number of rays, similar to standard volume rendering. However, the additional acoustic calculations (MIDI mapping, frequency conversion, buffer management) add constant overhead per sample. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the scalar field size and the ray buffer size. The HRTF convolution requires additional memory for impulse response coefficients. Performance: The method is computationally expensive compared to standard volume rendering due to the dual optical/acoustic processing. Strengths: Effective for detecting small changes in symmetry and vortex geometry that are hard to see visually; allows for background monitoring; complements visual analysis. Limitations: Requires user auditory training; limited by sampling resolution; computationally intensive. When to Use: When analyzing dynamic scalar fields for small local changes (e.g., superconductor fields) where visual fatigue or color perception limits are a bottleneck. When Not to Use: For users without auditory training or when real-time performance is critical and hardware is limited. Auditory Volume Rendering was presented at The 25th International Conference on Auditory Display (ICAD 2019) in June 2019. It builds on the concept of data sonification and the similarities between light and sound propagation models. The HyperVolume model was introduced to represent objects with both optical and auditory properties. The technique was demonstrated using a case study of superconductor field analysis, specifically looking at Abrikosov vortices. Implementation was done using C++/Python with VTK, OpenAL, and OpenCV. Visual-auditory Volume Rendering of Scalar Fields, https://doi.org/10.21785/icad2019.004, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Iterative Depth Volume Rendering (IDVR)
head: IDVR with Skip-Step Optimization, IDVR design
body: Iterative Depth Volume Rendering (IDVR) is an interactive volume rendering technique that removes the brain tissue in front of a clipping surface to expose deeper internal structures while retaining anatomical context. Unlike standard direct volume ray casting which composites all samples along a ray, IDVR iteratively searches for the closest valid voxel (V) or depth voxel (Vd) along view rays to determine depth and opacity, enabling observation of subcortical regions and white matter that surface-based visualizations miss. It distinguishes itself by using a skip-step optimization to manage the performance cost of searching for these closest valid voxels without early termination. IDVR operates by removing the brain volume in front of a clipping surface while rendering anatomical maps and volume change data completely. The core mechanism involves an iterative search for the Point of View/Projection (PV), defined as the closest valid voxel (V) or depth voxel (Vd) with the highest lighting/alpha value (la) along the view ray. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data texture TV, clipping surface definition, view ray parameters, skip-step parameter i. Output: Final pixel color and depth, with the front-most brain tissue removed to reveal internal structures. Data Structures: Texture TV: The volume data texture. Its resolution is assumed to be sufficiently large for the skip-step optimization to be effective. Skip-step parameter i: An integer controlling the accuracy and performance of the iteration. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, define the view ray and intersect it with the volume bounding box to determine the entry parameter t{near} and exit parameter t{far}. 2. Iterative Search: March along the ray segment [t{near}, t{far}] to seek the PV. 3. Skip-Step Optimization: Skip every i-th texel so it is not tested as a candidate for V or Vd. If i=1 (High Accuracy): Test every texel. If i=2 (Balanced): Skip every 2nd texel. If i=3 (Low Accuracy): Skip every 3rd texel. 4. Validity Check: For each tested texel, determine if it is a valid voxel (V) or depth voxel (Vd) relative to the clipping surface, and compute its lighting/alpha value (la). 5. Best Candidate Tracking: The iteration cannot be early-terminated because there is always a possibility of finding a closer V or Vd with a higher la value further along the ray. Track the candidate with the smallest depth t and highest la. 6. Compositing: Render the anatomical regions in front of the clipping surface and the surface texture to provide localization, blending their colors with the volume change data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def idvrrender(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, volumetexture, clippingsurface, skipstepi): """ Renders a single ray using Iterative Depth Volume Rendering. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector (x, y, z) raydirection: Normalized 3D vector (x, y, z) tnear: Entry parameter into volume bounding box tfar: Exit parameter from volume bounding box volumetexture: 3D array with.sampletrilinear(pos) method clippingsurface: Object with.isbehind(pos) method skipstepi: Integer skip-step parameter (1, 2, or 3) Returns: color: Final pixel color (r, g, b) alpha: Final pixel opacity depth: Depth of the closest valid voxel found """ # Step size derived from texture resolution stepsize = 1.0 / max(volumetexture.resolution) t = tnear texelindex = 0 bestdepth = float('inf') bestla = -1.0 bestcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) bestalpha = 0.0 while t <= tfar: # Skip-step optimization: skip every i-th texel if skipstepi > 1 and texelindex % skipstepi != 0: t += stepsize texelindex += 1 continue # Sample volume at current position pos = rayorigin + raydirection t vval = volumetexture.sampletrilinear(pos) # Check if voxel is behind clipping surface (valid V or Vd) isvalid = clippingsurface.isbehind(pos) if isvalid: # Standard transfer function mapping to extinction and color sigma = max(0.0, vval) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma stepsize) color = (vval, vval, vval) la = alpha # la represents visibility/opacity contribution # Update best candidate: closer to camera (smaller t) and higher la if t < bestdepth and la > bestla: bestdepth = t bestla = la bestcolor = color bestalpha = alpha t += stepsize texelindex += 1 # Composite with anatomical context to provide localization if bestalpha > 0: anatomicalcolor = (0.8, 0.8, 0.8) # Context texture color finalcolor = bestcolor bestalpha + anatomicalcolor (1.0 - bestalpha) finalalpha = bestalpha else: finalcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) finalalpha = 0.0 return finalcolor, finalalpha, bestdepth Parameters: i (Skip-step parameter): Controls the trade-off between accuracy and performance. i=1: High Accuracy. Tests every texel. i=2: Balanced. Skips every 2nd texel. Nearly no visual artifacts. i=3: Low Accuracy. Skips every 3rd texel. Noticeable artifacts (loose wrong depth values) but reasonable performance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visual Artifacts: When i=3, loose wrong depth values may appear due to skipped texels potentially being the true closest valid voxel. However, these artifacts do not disturb overall depth perception in the cutout. Performance Limitation: The iteration cannot be early-terminated because a closer valid voxel with higher la might exist further along the ray. This makes the method computationally expensive compared to standard ray casting with early termination. Time Complexity: The method requires iterating over all neighboring texels along the ray without early termination, making it O(N/i) where N is the number of samples along the ray. Memory Complexity: Depends on the volume texture size and the storage for the best candidate per ray. Measured Performance: Nvidia GeForce GTX 480 (Mono view, 1400x1050): i=1: 55 fps i=2: 11 fps i=3: 18 fps Nvidia Quadro 6000 (Stereo view, 1400x1050): i=1: 4 fps i=2: 3 fps i=3: 10 fps Strengths: Allows observation of data inside the brain, including subcortical regions and white matter, which surface-based visualization misses. Provides good spatial perception and anatomical localization through blending of colors. Limitations: Performance is limited by the iteration over all neighboring texels, which cannot be early-terminated. Frame rates are lower than common volume rendering, especially in stereo mode. When to use: When interactive visualization of internal brain structures (e.g., in neurodegenerative disease studies) is required, and the user needs to see past a clipping surface while retaining anatomical context. When not to use: When high performance is critical and visual artifacts from skipping texels are unacceptable, or when the volume data does not require internal structure visualization behind a clipping plane. IDVR was developed for the interactive 3D visualization of structural changes in the brain of a person with corticobasal syndrome (CBS). It was introduced to allow scientists to observe data not only on the surface but also inside the brain, providing a better impression of the spatial extent of regional volume loss in the context of individual brain anatomy. The work was funded by the Helmholtz Portfolio Theme “Supercomputing and Modeling for the Human Brain” and partially by the “Human Brain Project”. Interactive 3D visualization of structural changes in the brain of a person with corticobasal syndrome., https://archive.org/details/pubmed-PMC4017140, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Gradient-based Boundary Highlighting
head: Gradient magnitude opacity mask, Weighted Opacity Boundary Highlighting
body: Gradient-based Boundary Highlighting is a technique in direct volume ray casting that enhances the visibility of material interfaces by modulating the sample opacity with the normalized gradient magnitude of the volume density. It solves the problem of indistinct boundaries in homogeneous regions by treating the gradient magnitude as a measure of boundary "importance," ensuring that transitions between materials with differing optical properties are emphasized in the final image. Unlike discrete classification methods that produce sharp, 0-1 material decisions, this method yields a continuous result where boundaries are composited from the adjacent materials, reducing visual artifacts associated with hard segmentation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar density volume D, a set of K materials, each defined by a color \mathbf{c}k and an opacity \alphak, and a probability map pk(\mathbf{p}) for each material at every voxel. Output: A rendered image where material boundaries are highlighted via weighted opacity. Data Structures: Density Volume: A 3D grid of scalar values representing material density or intensity. Probability Maps: K 3D grids of scalar values, where each grid corresponds to the probability of a specific material existing at that location. The probabilities for all materials at a given voxel typically sum to 1. Global Gradient Statistics: Two scalar values, |G|{min} and |G|{max}, representing the global minimum and maximum gradient magnitudes computed over the entire volume. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Global Gradient Calculation): Compute the gradient magnitude |G(\mathbf{p})| for every voxel \mathbf{p} in the volume. The gradient \nabla D(\mathbf{p}) is typically computed using finite differences (e.g., central differences) on the density volume. The global extrema are determined: |G|{min} = \min{\mathbf{p}} |G(\mathbf{p})| |G|{max} = \max{\mathbf{p}} |G(\mathbf{p})| 2. Ray Marching: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. At each sample position \mathbf{p}i along the ray: 3. Gradient Normalization: Calculate the normalized gradient magnitude |Gs|' at the current sample position s (or \mathbf{p}i). This value ranges from 0 to 1, where 0 indicates the interior of a homogeneous material and 1 indicates a strong boundary: |Gs|' = \frac{|Gs| - |G|{min}}{|G|{max} - |G|{min}} 4. Weighted Opacity Calculation: Compute the effective opacity \alphas for the sample by combining the material probabilities, their base opacities, and the normalized gradient magnitude. This blends the contributions of all K materials present at the sample location, weighted by their likelihood and the boundary strength: \alphas = \left( \sum{k=1}^{K} \alphak pk \right) \cdot |Gs|' Here, \alphak is the opacity of material k, and pk is the probability of material k at the sample position. 5. Color Calculation: Compute the base color \mathbf{c}s for the sample using the weighted sum of material colors: \mathbf{c}s = \frac{\sum{k=1}^{K} \mathbf{c}k \alphak pk}{\sum{k=1}^{K} \alphak pk} (Note: The source defines the weighted opacity formula but implies standard weighted color blending for the color component to maintain continuity. If the denominator is zero, \mathbf{c}s is undefined or set to background.) 6. Compositing: Composite the sample (\mathbf{c}s, \alphas) into the accumulated color and opacity using the front-to-back volume rendering equation: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}s \cdot \alphas \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphas Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gradientbasedboundaryhighlighting(volume, materials, numsamples): """ volume: 3D array of density values materials: list of dicts, each with 'color' (RGB), 'opacity' (scalar), 'probabilities' (3D array) numsamples: number of samples per ray Returns: rendered image """ # Precompute global gradient statistics # Compute gradient magnitude for the entire volume gradmag = computegradientmagnitude(volume) gmin = np.min(gradmag) gmax = np.max(gradmag) # Handle division by zero if volume is constant if gmax == gmin: gmax = gmin + 1e-8 # Initialize output image height, width = volume.shape[:2] # Assuming 2D slice or projection for simplicity # In full 3D ray casting, this loop iterates over pixels image = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Define ray (omitted for brevity, assumes ray origin o and direction d) # Intersect ray with volume bounding box to get tnear, tfar tnear, tfar = intersectrayvolume(o, d, volumebounds) dt = (tfar - tnear) / numsamples cacc = 0.0 aacc = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): t = tnear + i dt p = o + t d # Sample position # 1. Get density and compute gradient magnitude at p # Note: In practice, interpolate density from volume density = interpolatevolume(volume, p) gradmagval = interpolatevolume(gradmag, p) # 2. Normalize gradient magnitude gnorm = (gradmagval - gmin) / (gmax - gmin) gnorm = np.clip(gnorm, 0.0, 1.0) # 3. Compute weighted opacity and color # Sum over K materials weightedalphasum = 0.0 weightedcolorsum = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) for mat in materials: # Interpolate probability for this material at p prob = interpolatevolume(mat['probabilities'], p) alphak = mat['opacity'] colork = mat['color'] term = alphak prob weightedalphasum += term weightedcolorsum += colork term # Avoid division by zero if weightedalphasum > 1e-8: cs = weightedcolorsum / weightedalphasum else: cs = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # Apply gradient mask to opacity alphas = weightedalphasum gnorm # 4. Front-to-back compositing # alphas is the opacity of the current sample segment # cs is the color of the current sample segment # Update accumulator # Cout = sum(ci alphai product(1-alphaj)) # alphaout = 1 - product(1-alphai) # Iterative form: # Cacc <- Cacc + (1 - alphaacc) cs alphas # alphaacc <- alphaacc + (1 - alphaacc) alphas cacc = cacc + (1.0 - aacc) cs alphas aacc = aacc + (1.0 - aacc) alphas # Early ray termination optimization (optional) if aacc > 0.99: break image[y, x] = cacc return image def computegradientmagnitude(volume): # Compute gradient using central differences # dx, dy, dz are gradients dx = np.gradient(volume, axis=0) dy = np.gradient(volume, axis=1) dz = np.gradient(volume, axis=2) # Magnitude mag = np.sqrt(dx2 + dy2 + dz2) return mag Parameters: |G|{max}: Global maximum gradient magnitude. Used for normalization. |G|{min}: Global minimum gradient magnitude. Used for normalization. K: Number of materials. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise Sensitivity: The gradient magnitude is inherently sensitive to noise in the volume data. However, the method relies on a "neighborhood weighted classification" process that produces homogeneous material regions, which mitigates noise by ensuring the gradient magnitude aligns with actual material opacity values rather than high-frequency noise artifacts. Constant Regions: If the volume has no variation (|G|{max} = |G|{min}), normalization fails. A small epsilon should be added to the denominator. Boundary Importance: The method assumes that a larger gradient magnitude corresponds to a more "important" boundary. If two materials have similar opacities, the boundary gradient will be small, potentially making the boundary less visible, which is the intended behavior for "soft" transitions. A variant that applies opacity masks to hatching strokes to ensure they only appear where they support contour and suggestive contour lines. It calculates an opacity Oh based on the light gradient direction \mathbf{k}, view vector \mathbf{v}, normal \mathbf{n}, and a threshold \thetac. The weight wa maps the angle between the normal and view vector to [0,1] using a clamped arccosine function: wa = \text{clamp}{[0,1]} \left( \frac{\arccos(-\langle \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v} \rangle) - \thetac}{\frac{1}{2}\pi - \thetac} \right). The final opacity is Oh = \max(wa \cdot wk \cdot F, 0), where wk weights the light gradient dependence on view and F is a scaling factor. A pitfall is that \mathbf{k} is not normalized to account for curvature magnitude. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K) per sample, where N is the number of samples per ray and K is the number of materials. The preprocessing step requires O(V) where V is the number of voxels to compute global gradients. Memory Complexity: O(V \cdot K) to store probability maps for K materials, plus O(V) for the gradient magnitude volume. Strengths: Produces continuous, visually pleasing boundaries without hard segmentation artifacts. It highlights material interfaces based on their visual importance (gradient magnitude). Limitations: Sensitive to noise if the underlying volume is not smooth or if classification is not robust. Requires pre-computed probability maps for each material. The global normalization (|G|{min}, |G|{max}) may not adapt well to local variations in boundary importance across different parts of the volume. When to use: When the goal is to visualize material interfaces in multi-material volumes where discrete segmentation is undesirable or inaccurate. When not to use: When noise is high and cannot be filtered, or when local boundary importance varies significantly and global normalization obscures local features. The method was introduced in the context of multivolume visualization for spatially aligned volumes after 3D/3D image registration. It contrasts with "class decision methods" which use 0-1 procedures resulting in discrete rendering, offering a more continual result by composing boundaries from two materials. The approach builds on the idea that gradient magnitude magnifies at material boundaries and equals zero in the interior of homogeneous materials, corresponding to the first derivative of separated materials. A multivolume visualization method for spatially aligned volumes after 3D/3D image registration, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.irbm.2011.01.040, fetched 2026-10-26 Sline: Seamless Line Illustration for Interactive Biomedical Visualization, https://doi.org/10.2312/vcbm.20161281, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Perceptually Linear Transfer Function
head: JND-based Transfer Function, Perceptual Transfer Function, Perceptually Linear Transfer Function for Direct Volume Rendering
body: The Perceptually Linear Transfer Function maps volume density values to transfer function inputs such that the resulting rendered intensities are linear in Just Noticeable Difference (JND) space, optimizing the use of High Dynamic Range (HDR) display contrast for human perception. Unlike methods that specify transfer functions on a logarithmic scale to address exponential transparency alone, this method accounts for the non-linear sensitivity of the human visual system at different luminance levels, ensuring that equal steps in the transfer function correspond to equal perceptual steps in the final image. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Original volume densities \rho0 from the dataset. Output: Transformed density values \rho specified in JND space, which serve as the input to the opacity transfer function during rendering. Data Structures: The method relies on the JND function f{JND} defined by the DICOM Grayscale Standard Display Function. This function maps physical intensity values to perceptual units (JNDs). Its inverse, f{JND}^{-1}, maps intensity values to just noticeable differences. Formulas: The emission-absorption rendering equation for a segment from a to b is defined as: I(a, b) = \inta^b C\rho(u) \cdot e^{-\inta^u \tau\rho(t)dt} du where: C is the emission constant (emitted energy per unit length). \tau is the absorption constant (absorption per unit length). \rho(u) is the volume density at point u. Assuming constant density over a segment, the equation simplifies to: I(a, b) = \frac{C\alpha}{\tau} with opacity \alpha defined as: \alpha:= 1 - e^{-\inta^u \tau\rho(t)dt} The perceived intensity in JND space is calculated as: I{perceived}(a, b) = f{JND}(I(a, b)) = f{JND}\left(\frac{C\alpha}{\tau}\right) To achieve perceptual linearity, the densities \rho are specified as: \rho:= \log(f{JND}^{-1}(\rho0)) This mapping ensures that original volume densities \rho0 are mapped approximately linearly to just noticeable intensity differences in the final image. Steps: 1. Retrieve the original volume density \rho0 for a given data value. 2. Apply the inverse JND function f{JND}^{-1} to \rho0 to determine the corresponding physical intensity level. 3. Take the logarithm of the result to compute the transformed density \rho. 4. Use \rho as the input to the opacity transfer function during rendering. Parameters: C: Emission constant. \tau: Absorption constant. f{JND}: The JND function from the DICOM Grayscale Standard Display Function. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-constant Density: Volume densities are not constant along the ray in practice. Consequently, changing a segment of the transfer function while others remain the same can still result in non-linear actual intensity changes on the screen. However, the correspondence between the transfer function and the display response is more direct and easier to control than without this mapping. Color: The basic formulation considers only intensity JNDs and ignores color. In practical applications, color is an important factor, but the core method described focuses on intensity linearity. Complexity: The method requires evaluating the inverse JND function and a logarithm for each density value. The complexity is dominated by the lookup or evaluation of f{JND}^{-1}, which is typically a piecewise function or a lookup table defined by the DICOM standard. Strengths: Optimizes the use of HDR display contrast for human perception. Provides a more direct and controllable mapping between transfer function adjustments and perceptual changes in the final image compared to linear or simple logarithmic scales. Limitations: Does not inherently account for color perception. The assumption of constant density along the ray is an approximation; actual rendering may exhibit non-linearities if the density varies significantly within a segment. When to use: When using HDR displays and the goal is to maximize perceptual contrast and control over the rendered image's intensity distribution. The method was proposed in the paper "Volume Rendering for High Dynamic Range Displays" by Ghosh, Trentacoste, and Heidrich. It addresses the limitations of conventional display systems (CRT/LCD) with dynamic ranges of about 400:1 and maximum intensities of ~300 cd/m², by adapting transfer functions for HDR displays with dynamic ranges up to 50,000:1 and maximum intensities of 2,700 cd/m². The work builds upon previous observations by Potts and Möller regarding logarithmic scales for exponential transparency, extending it to include human visual sensitivity. Volume Rendering for High Dynamic Range Displays, https://vccimaging.org/Publications/Ghosh2005VRH/Ghosh2005VRH.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Optimization and Coherence Techniques
body: Optimization and Coherence Techniques encompass methods that improve the performance and visual quality of direct volume ray casting by leveraging spatial, temporal, or structural redundancies in the data or rendering process. These techniques address the high computational cost of ray traversal and sampling by reducing redundant memory accesses, filtering artifacts dynamically, or adapting the sampling strategy based on local data properties. They differ from sibling methods like Adaptive Undersampling or Slice-based and Proxy Geometry Rendering by focusing on the efficiency of the ray-casting loop itself—specifically through cache management, page table optimization, and on-the-fly geometric analysis—rather than changing the fundamental integration order or proxy geometry representation. The methods in this family share the following core mechanisms and constraints: 1. Ray Traversal Optimization: All methods operate within the standard ray marching loop defined in Direct volume ray casting. They modify the sampling, interpolation, or compositing steps to reduce computational overhead or improve visual fidelity without altering the fundamental front-to-back integration equation. 2. Data Locality and Coherence: Techniques exploit the spatial coherence of volume data, where successive samples along a ray often access nearby memory locations or map to the same page table entries. This allows for caching of look-up results and reduction of cache misses. 3. Dynamic Adaptation: Several methods dynamically adjust the rendering process based on the data content. This includes cutting planes that clip the ray traversal, region growing that filters artifacts based on connectivity, and cache management that adapts to missing data blocks. 4. Memory Management: For large-scale data, techniques manage memory access patterns through block caches, page tables, and hash tables to handle data that does not fit in main memory, ensuring scalability to petascale or exascale datasets. Koyamada's Algorithm is an image-order ray-casting method for unstructured tetrahedral volumes that leverages image-space coherency to generate and compose ray-segments in object space. It differs from its siblings by explicitly constructing continuous ray-segments via scan-conversion of external faces and traversing them through the volume using cell connectivity, rather than sampling fixed intervals along a pixel ray. Cutting Plane Integration is an interactive volume rendering technique that dynamically slices a 3D dataset using a semi-transparent geometric plane to reveal internal structures. It builds on Direct volume ray casting by modifying the ray traversal and compositing stages to respect the cutting plane boundary. Ray casting with on-the-fly region growing extends direct volume ray casting by integrating a local region growing algorithm during ray traversal to eliminate artifacts caused by contrast inhomogeneities, such as isolated "particle-like" regions in medical imaging. Unlike standard ray casting which may render these artifacts as part of the surface, or undersampling which loses local features, this approach filters small isolated noise while preserving large structural boundaries like endocardial walls. It is specifically designed for 3-D navigation in cardiac MSCT data where contrast distribution is non-uniform. Definition: Reporting cache misses during ray-casting for unmapped page table entries, using a hash table shared among rays to distribute misses over frames. Step: Each ray stores cache miss block IDs into a hash table shared with other rays using atomic writes. The ray-caster tracks an 'in use' bit for every block in the block cache to allow the LRU caching strategy to track usage. The cache miss hash tables and cache usage are read back from the GPU to the CPU once per rendering frame. Parameter: Block ID size is 32-bit for small blocks of 32^3 voxels (addressing up to 128 teravoxels) or 64-bit for scaling up to exascale. M is the maximum number of cache misses tracked per ray from front to back (e.g., M = 4); misses farther back are not reported in the same frame. Layout: One hash table is allocated for each pixel tile of size N \times N in screen space (e.g., N = 64). Each hash table is an array with a fixed maximum number of entries per row. Pitfall: If a target row in the hash table is full, the cache miss is dropped. Dropped misses are reported in a later frame if the block is still visible. Number: Reading back 300 KB of state for a screen resolution of 1024 \times 1024 and a block cache size of 1GB takes less than 1ms. Definition: An optimization to reduce page table look-up overhead by reusing results from previous samples when successive samples map to the same page directory/table entries. Step: The ray-casting loop tracks the indices of the last used page directory/table entries. When the next sample along a ray maps to the same entry, the result of the look-up from the previous sample is re-used instead of fetching the entry again. Number: For b{pt} = b{vox} = 32 and t = 2, for an axis-aligned ray, the page table is accessed only every 32 voxels, and the page directory every 1024 voxels. The techniques described in this family originate from the need to render petascale and exascale volume datasets interactively. The work by Hadwiger et al. (2012) introduced these methods to handle microscopy data streams where data cannot fit entirely in main memory. The cache miss reporting and page table optimization techniques were developed to manage sparse data access patterns efficiently on GPUs, distributing the latency of data fetching over multiple frames to maintain smooth frame rates. The region growing technique was developed for medical imaging applications, specifically cardiac MSCT, to handle contrast inhomogeneities without pre-segmentation. PDF Interactive Volume Exploration of Petascale Microscopy Data Streams..., https://vccvisualization.org/publications/2012hadwigerpetascale.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Koyamada's Algorithm
head: Koyamada's DVR algorithm, Sequential DVR Algorithm
body: Koyamada's Algorithm is an image-order ray-casting method for unstructured tetrahedral volumes that leverages image-space coherency to generate and compose ray-segments in object space. It differs from its siblings by explicitly constructing continuous ray-segments via scan-conversion of external faces and traversing them through the volume using cell connectivity, rather than sampling fixed intervals along a pixel ray. Inputs: Volumetric dataset defined by tetrahedral cells. Outputs: A composited image where each pixel contains the final color and opacity derived from the composited ray-segments stored in the RayBuffer. Data Structures: The algorithm uses three primary data structures: 1. VertexArray: Stores per-vertex data. scalarvalue: The scalar value at the vertex. WSC: World Space Coordinates (x, y, z). NPC: Normalized Projection Coordinates (x, y, z) on the screen plane. 2. CellArray: Stores per-cell topology. Vertices: An array of 4 integers, containing the indices of the four vertices of the tetrahedron. NeighborCells: An array of 4 integers. Each entry corresponds to a face of the tetrahedron. If the face is internal, the value is the index of the neighbor cell. The index within the neighbor cell's NeighborCells array that refers back to the current cell is also stored (typically encoded or derived to avoid search). If the face is external, a sentinel value (e.g., -1) is used. 3. RayBuffer: A 2D virtual array indexed by pixel coordinates (u, v). Each entry holds a linked list of composited ray-segments. Each list element contains: ZDepth: The z-coordinate (in NPC) of the exit point of the ray-segment. Lists are maintained in increasing order of this value. Color-Opacity: The composited RGB color and opacity value for the segment. Algorithm Steps: 1. Generate Ray-Segments (Scan Conversion): Iterate through all front-facing (ff) external faces of the volume in any order. For each ff-external face, scan-convert its projection onto the screen. For each pixel (u, v) covered by the face's projection: Determine the ray origin and direction corresponding to pixel (u, v). Calculate the entry point P into the volume. The entry point is the intersection of the ray with the ff-external face. Initialize the composition state at P (typically starting with background color/opacity). Traverse the ray through the volume cells until it exits through a back-facing (bf) external face. Insert the resulting composited ray-segment into the linked list of the RayBuffer at pixel (u, v). 2. Trace Ray Inside Volume (Cell Traversal): Given an entry point P and entry face F{in} for a tetrahedral cell C:. Identify the three other faces of C that are candidates for the exit face. For each candidate face F{cand}: Let the vertices of F{cand} be A, C, D (where A is a common vertex with F{in} or chosen appropriately to define the triangle). Check if the ray intersects the plane of F{cand}. If the projection of vectors \vec{AC} and \vec{AD} onto the screen are parallel, the face is perpendicular to the screen; skip this face and test the next candidate. Otherwise, calculate the intersection point Q of the ray with the plane of F{cand}. Validate if Q lies inside the triangle ACD using barycentric coordinates. 3. Determine Exit Face and Point: Express vector \vec{AQ} as a linear combination of \vec{AC} and \vec{AD}: \vec{AQ} = \alpha \vec{AC} + \beta \vec{AD} Solve for \alpha and \beta using the 2x2 linear system derived from the NPC coordinates: \begin{bmatrix} xC - xA & xD - xA \\ yC - yA & yD - yA \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \alpha \\ \beta \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} xr - xA \\ yr - yA \end{bmatrix} Where (xA, yA), (xC, yC), and (xD, yD) are the NPC coordinates of vertices A, C, D, and (xr, yr) are the NPC coordinates of the ray (constant for the pixel). Validate the intersection: If \alpha > 0, \beta > 0, and \alpha + \beta < 1, then Q is inside triangle ACD. This face is the exit face. No further tests are needed for this ray-segment within this cell. Otherwise, Q is not inside the triangle; test the next candidate face. If no candidate face yields a valid intersection, the ray exits through a back-facing external face (or the cell is degenerate). 4. Calculate Exit Properties: Once the exit face and point Q are identified, calculate the z-coordinate of Q in NPC space: zQ = zA + \alpha(zC - zA) - \beta(zD - zA) Note: The source formula uses a minus sign for the \beta term; ensure consistency with the vector definition \vec{AQ} = \alpha \vec{AC} + \beta \vec{AD}. If the standard barycentric form is used, the sign may vary based on vertex ordering. The source explicitly states: zQ = zA + \alpha(zC - zA) - \beta(zD - zA). Calculate the scalar value sQ at Q using 2D inverse distance interpolation (barycentric interpolation): sQ = \alpha sC + \beta sD + (1 - \alpha - \beta) sA Where sA, sC, sD are the scalar values at vertices A, C, D. The coefficients represent the area ratios of sub-triangles QAD, QAC, and QCD to the area of triangle ACD. 5. Resample and Composite: With the entry point P (known from the previous step or scan conversion) and exit point Q (just calculated), resample the scalar values along the segment PQ. Use equi-distant sampling with interval \Delta s. \Delta s must be small enough to ensure at least one sample is taken in each cell. Composite the samples using standard volume rendering integration (e.g., front-to-back compositing) to update the color and opacity. The exit point Q and its properties become the entry point for the next cell. Repeat steps 2-5 until a back-facing external face is reached. 6. Final Composition: After all ff-external faces are processed, the RayBuffer contains all composited ray-segments. For each pixel, sort the linked list of ray-segments by ZDepth (if not already sorted during insertion) and composite them from front to back to produce the final pixel color and opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def koyamadaalgorithm(vertices, cells, screenwidth, screenheight): # Initialize RayBuffer: 2D virtual array of linked lists raybuffer = [[[] for in range(screenheight)] for in range(screenwidth)] # 1. Generate Ray-Segments via scan-conversion of ff-external faces for face in externalfaces: if not isfrontfacing(face): continue # Scan-convert face projection onto screen for pixelu, pixelv in scanconvert(face): rayorigin, raydir = getray(pixelu, pixelv) entrypoint = intersectrayface(rayorigin, raydir, face) currentcell = findcellcontaining(entrypoint) currentface = getentryface(currentcell, entrypoint) color, opacity = backgroundcolor, 0.0 # 2-5. Trace ray inside volume while not isbackfacingexternal(currentface): exitpoint, exitface = traceraythroughcell( currentcell, currentface, entrypoint, rayorigin, raydir) segmentcolor, segmentopacity = resampleandcomposite( entrypoint, exitpoint, currentcell) color, opacity = compositefronttoback( color, opacity, segmentcolor, segmentopacity) currentcell = neighborcell(currentcell, currentface, exitface) currentface = exitface entrypoint = exitpoint raybuffer[pixelu][pixelv].append( RaySegment(zdepth=exitpoint.z, color=color, opacity=opacity)) # 6. Final Composition for u in range(screenwidth): for v in range(screenheight): raybuffer[u][v].sort(key=lambda seg: seg.zdepth) finalcolor, finalopacity = compositeraysegments(raybuffer[u][v]) setpixel(u, v, finalcolor, finalopacity) return raybuffer Parameters: Sampling Interval (\Delta s): Equi-distant sampling is used. The value must be chosen such that \Delta s is small enough to guarantee at least one sample per cell. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sorting Order: The original algorithm sorts ff-external faces by centroid x-coordinates, which is an approximate order that may be incorrect. The modified approach described here avoids this by scan-converting faces in any order and generating rays per pixel, ensuring correctness. Parallel Vectors: If the projection of vectors \vec{AC} and \vec{AD} are parallel, the face is perpendicular to the screen, and the ray cannot exit through that face in the projected sense. Test another face. Precision: Barycentric coordinate validation (\alpha > 0, \beta > 0, \alpha + \beta < 1) is sensitive to floating-point precision. Use a small epsilon for comparisons. It handles spatial decomposition constraints within a single processing unit by treating local clusters as a single local subvolume, ensuring continuous ray-segments across pseudo-boundary faces. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Leverages image-space coherency, reducing redundant calculations. Handles unstructured tetrahedral grids efficiently using connectivity information. Avoids the sorting pitfalls of the original algorithm. Limitations: Requires efficient scan-conversion of external faces. The RayBuffer can become large for complex volumes with many external faces. The quality of the image depends on the sampling interval \Delta s. When to Use: Suitable for unstructured tetrahedral volumes where image-space coherency can be exploited. name: Local Rendering Phase
body: The Local Rendering Phase is the core computation step in the Object-Space (OS) parallel implementation of Koyamada's Algorithm. It solves the problem of redundant ray-segment generation that occurs when local clusters on a single processor are treated as independent subvolumes. By treating the set of local clusters assigned to a processor as a single local subvolume, it ensures that ray-segments crossing pseudo-boundary faces (shared between local clusters) are composed into a single continuous segment rather than being recomputed. This phase builds on Koyamada's Algorithm by handling the spatial decomposition constraints within a single processing unit. Inputs: The set of local clusters Cp assigned to processor Pi. The CellArray structures containing cell geometry and connectivity for these clusters. The RayBuffer structure for the current pixel row/column being processed. Outputs: Composited color and opacity values for ray-segments exiting the local subvolume, stored in the RayBuffer. Data Structures: CellArray: Contains cell data with neighbor references. ClusterData: Preserves connectivity information between cells despite clustering. RayBuffer: A linked-list structure indexed by pixel location, where each entry stores a list of ray-segments sorted by their exit z-value. Steps: 1. Concurrent Traversal: Each processor Pi concurrently traverses the cells of the CellArray structures of its local clusters Cp. 2. Face Classification: For each cell ci in Cp, check each face f. Identify f as an external face if cell ci does not have a neighbor cell through face f. Identify f as a boundary face if cell ci is neighbor to a cell cj through face f such that cj belongs to a non-local cluster of Pi. Faces shared between two local clusters of Pi are pseudo-boundary faces and are skipped for ray generation. 3. Ray-Segment Generation: Scan-convert each identified external and boundary face. Generate a ray-segment for each pixel covered by the face. 4. Ray Traversal: Follow each generated ray-segment through the local subvolume according to Koyamada's algorithm. The traversal uses the connectivity information preserved in ClusterData structures, allowing the ray to pass through multiple local clusters seamlessly. The ray continues until it exits from a boundary-external face or a boundary-boundary face. 5. Buffer Insertion: When a ray-segment exits the local subvolume, insert its composited color and opacity values into the linked-list of the respective pixel location in the RayBuffer structure. Insertion must be in sorted order according to the ray-segment's exit z-value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def localrenderingphase(processorid, localclusters, cellarrays, raybuffer): """ Renders the local subvolume defined by localclusters for processorid. """ # Step 1 & 2: Traverse cells and classify faces rayorigins = [] for cluster in localclusters: for cell in cellarrays[cluster]: for face in cell.faces: if not face.hasneighbor(): rayorigins.append((cell, face, 'external')) elif face.neighbor.clusterid not in localclusters: rayorigins.append((cell, face, 'boundary')) # Pseudo-boundary faces (neighbor in localclusters) are skipped # Step 3, 4 & 5: Generate, trace, and buffer ray-segments for cell, face, facetype in rayorigins: pixels = scanconvertface(face) for pixel in pixels: # Initialize ray-segment parameters rayorigin = face.center raydirection = face.normal stepsize = cell.edgelength alpha = 0.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] currentcell = cell exitz = 0.0 # Step 4: Trace through local subvolume while True: # Sample cell data and perform front-to-back compositing density = currentcell.sample(rayorigin, raydirection) alphacell = density stepsize colorcell = currentcell.color(density) alphaout = alpha + (1.0 - alpha) alphacell colorout = color + (1.0 - alpha) colorcell alphacell alpha = alphaout color = colorout # Move to next cell along ray direction nextcell = currentcell.getneighborindirection(raydirection) if nextcell is None: exitz = rayorigin.z + stepsize break if nextcell.clusterid not in localclusters: exitz = rayorigin.z + stepsize break currentcell = nextcell rayorigin += raydirection stepsize # Step 5: Insert into RayBuffer sorted by exit z-value raybuffer.insertsorted(pixel, exitz, color, alpha) def scanconvertface(face): """ Rasterizes a polygonal face to return a list of covered pixel coordinates. """ return face.boundingbox.rasterize() Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Virtual Non-Convexities: Object-Space (OS) decomposition may create local subvolumes with virtual non-convexities, even if the global dataset is convex. This increases the number of ray-segments generated per pixel compared to the sequential algorithm. RayBuffer Necessity: Due to virtual non-convexities, multiple ray-segments may exit the local subvolume for a single pixel. The RayBuffer structure is crucial for handling this multiplicity and maintaining correct depth sorting. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on the RayBuffer size, which scales with the number of ray-segments per pixel. Virtual non-convexities can increase this number. Strengths: Eliminates redundant computation on pseudo-boundary faces by treating local clusters as a single subvolume. Limitations: Virtual non-convexities from decomposition can lead to more ray-segments per pixel than in the sequential case, requiring robust RayBuffer management. When to use: When implementing OS parallel direct volume rendering using Koyamada's Algorithm. The Local Rendering Phase was introduced in the context of parallel direct volume rendering of unstructured grids based on object-space decomposition. It addresses the inefficiencies of rendering local clusters independently by recognizing that clusters on the same processor are highly interacting and should be rendered as a unified local subvolume. name: Cutting Plane Integration
head: CuttingPlaneRender, Interactive Cutting Plane
body: Cutting Plane Integration is an interactive volume rendering technique that dynamically slices a 3D dataset using a semi-transparent geometric plane to reveal internal structures. It builds on Direct volume ray casting by modifying the ray traversal and compositing stages to respect the cutting plane boundary. The method integrates a cutting plane into the ray casting loop. The plane is defined by a position and orientation, and optionally a near-clip constraint. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data V, camera parameters (\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}), transfer function T, cutting plane definition (position \mathbf{g}0, normal \mathbf{n}, rotation angles), and near-clip plane definition (optional). Output: Final pixel color \mathbf{C}{out} and accumulated opacity \alpha{out}. Data Structures: Volume: 3D grid of scalar values. Cutting Plane: Defined by a world-space point \mathbf{g}0 and normal vector \mathbf{n}. The position is mapped from a normalized height parameter h \in [0, 1]. Ray State: Current position \mathbf{p}, accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc}, accumulated opacity \alpha{acc}. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Ray: For each pixel, define ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} and intersect with the volume bounding box to find entry t{near} and exit t{far}. 2. Define Cutting Plane: Map normalized height h to world Z position: z{plane} = 200 - 400 \cdot h. Apply rotation: convert degrees to radians and add a \pi radian offset to the Y-rotation if renderAbove is true. The plane equation is \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{g}0) = 0. 3. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to N-1: Calculate sample position \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{d}. Cutting Plane Check: Let \mathbf{g}{in} = \mathbf{p}i and \mathbf{g}{out} = \mathbf{p}{i+1} in world space. If (\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{g}{in} - \mathbf{g}0)) and (\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{g}{out} - \mathbf{g}0)) have opposite signs, the ray intersects the plane. Calculate the exact intersection point \mathbf{g}^ using linear interpolation. Find the corresponding volume-space point \mathbf{p}^ by solving \phi(\mathbf{p}^) - \mathbf{g}^ = 0 using a root-finding algorithm. Near-Clip Plane Check (Optional): If defined, count ray-surface intersections; an odd count indicates the near plane is inside the volume. Sampling: Retrieve V(\mathbf{p}i) and compute \mathbf{c}i, \alphai using the transfer function. Compositing: Update accumulators: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphai 4. Output: Set \mathbf{C}{out} = \mathbf{C}{acc}, \alpha{out} = \alpha{acc}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def cuttingplaneintegration(volumedata, volumebounds, cameraorigin, cameradir, planeheight, planerotx, planeroty, renderabove, transferfn, numsamples): # 1. Define cutting plane geometry zplane = 200.0 - 400.0 planeheight g0 = [0.0, 0.0, zplane] n = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] # Apply rotation around X axis cosx, sinx = math.cos(planerotx), math.sin(planerotx) n = [n[0], n[1]cosx - n[2]sinx, n[1]sinx + n[2]cosx] # Apply rotation around Y axis roty = planeroty if renderabove: roty += math.pi cosy, siny = math.cos(roty), math.sin(roty) n = [n[0]cosy + n[2]siny, n[1], -n[0]siny + n[2]cosy] # Normalize normal norm = math.sqrt(n[0]2 + n[1]2 + n[2]2) n = [n[0]/norm, n[1]/norm, n[2]/norm] # 2. Ray casting loop cacc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] aacc = 0.0 # Intersect ray with volume bounding box tnear, tfar = intersectaabb(cameraorigin, cameradir, volumebounds) if tnear > tfar: return cacc, aacc dt = (tfar - tnear) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples): t = tnear + i dt pcurr = [cameraorigin[j] + cameradir[j] t for j in range(3)] tnext = t + dt pnext = [cameraorigin[j] + cameradir[j] tnext for j in range(3)] # Cutting plane check valcurr = n[0](pcurr[0]-g0[0]) + n[1](pcurr[1]-g0[1]) + n[2](pcurr[2]-g0[2]) valnext = n[0](pnext[0]-g0[0]) + n[1](pnext[1]-g0[1]) + n[2](pnext[2]-g0[2]) if valcurr valnext < 0: # Intersection found, clip ray at intersection tint = t + dt (valcurr / (valcurr - valnext)) tfar = tint break # Sample volume (standard trilinear interpolation) vval = samplevolume(volumedata, volumebounds, pcurr) color, alpha = transferfn(vval) # Compositing cacc = [cacc[j] + (1.0 - aacc) color[j] alpha for j in range(3)] aacc = aacc + (1.0 - aacc) alpha return cacc, aacc def intersectaabb(origin, direction, bounds): tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bounds[i2] or origin[i] > bounds[i2+1]: return float('inf'), float('-inf') else: t1 = (bounds[i2] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bounds[i2+1] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmax < tmin: return float('inf'), float('-inf') return tmin, tmax def samplevolume(data, bounds, point): # Maps point to voxel coordinates and performs trilinear interpolation return 0.5 Parameters: planeHeight: Normalized float [0, 1] mapping to the Z-axis position. planeRotX, planeRotY: Rotation angles in degrees around the X and Y axes. renderAbove: Boolean flag that flips the plane 180° around Y when true. Edge Cases: Precision: Root finding for near-clip planes requires careful initialization (e.g., x0 = p{in} + \epsilon \frac{p{out} - p{in}}{\|p{out} - p{in}\|{L2}}) to ensure convergence. Boundaries: Large pixel frustums may cause ray-surface intersections at block boundaries; root finding methods remain pixel-accurate in these cases. Region of Interest (ROI) rendering is a technique to visualize internal features by defining a specific region and rendering only that portion of the dataset. It solves the problem where full opacity is obtained before reaching internal structures of interest, such as seeds within pulp, by isolating the target volume. Unlike standard clipping which often uses global planes, ROI rendering supports arbitrary geometric envelopes, masks, and intensity-based automatic detection. This variant uses a root-finding based method to realize cutting planes and near-clip planes during volume rendering compositing. For near-clip planes, since rendering is water-tight, an odd number of ray-surface intersections indicates the near plane is inside the volume. The intersection point g^ \in G is determined using trivial formulas, and the corresponding point p^ \in P is found by solving \phi(p^) - g^ = 0 using a root-finding algorithm (e.g., Newton-Raphson). Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray N and the number of pixels. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the volume size for storage. Strengths: Real-time interactivity and simple plane intersection test. Limitations: Limited to planar cuts; root finding requires proper initialization. The theoretical basis for pixel-accurate cutting and near-clipping using root-finding methods is described in research on isogeometric volume visualization. Implementation details regarding normalized height mapping and interactive plane manipulation are documented in unofficial projects. name: Region of Interest (ROI) Rendering
head: Clipping in Volume Rendering, ROI Rendering, Region of Interest (ROI) Mode, Sub-volume Rendering
body: Region of Interest (ROI) rendering is a technique to visualize internal features by defining a specific region and rendering only that portion of the dataset. It solves the problem where full opacity is obtained before reaching internal structures of interest, such as seeds within pulp, by isolating the target volume. Unlike standard clipping which often uses global planes, ROI rendering supports arbitrary geometric envelopes, masks, and intensity-based automatic detection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset V, Region of Interest definition (geometric primitives, mask volume, or Point of Interest), rendering parameters (transfer function, ray step size). Output: Rendered image containing only the voxels within the defined ROI. Data Structures: Geometric ROI: Defined by camera near/far clipping planes, six orthographic clipping planes (rectangular subvolume), arbitrarily oriented half-space clipping planes, or closed geometric objects. Mask ROI: Auxiliary binary volume M where values indicate inclusion/exclusion. Intensity ROI: Defined by a Point of Interest (POI) and a radius R derived from intensity thresholds along cast rays. Steps: 1. Define ROI: Select one of the methods above. 2. Ray Clipping (Image-Order): For each pixel, generate a ray r(t) = O + tD. Clip the ray against all geometric region definitions as a preprocessing step. Determine the valid interval [t{start}, t{end}] where the ray intersects the ROI. If no intersection, skip the ray. 3. Sample Evaluation: Evaluate the ray function only along segments of the ray that are within the region of interest. For each sample point p along the ray: If using a mask volume M, consult M(p) to determine if its contribution should be included or excluded. If using geometric clipping, check if p is inside the defined geometry. If using intensity-based ROI, check if distance from POI \le R and intensity conditions are met. 4. Compositing: Accumulate color and opacity for samples that pass the ROI check. For object-order methods, determine for each sample whether it is within the region of interest before incorporating its contribution into the image. If the underlying graphics hardware is being utilized for the object-order volume rendering as is the case with a texture mapping approach, hardware clipping planes may be available to help support regions of interest. volorigin[i]) / voldir[i] t2 = (1.0 - volorigin[i]) / voldir[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Clip against ROI planes if provided tstart, tend = tmin, tmax if roiplanes is not None: for plane in roiplanes: denom = plane.normal[0]voldir[0] + plane.normal[1]voldir[1] + plane.normal[2]voldir[2] if abs(denom) > 1e-6: tclip = (plane.dist - (plane.normal[0]volorigin[0] + plane.normal[1]volorigin[1] + plane.normal[2]volorigin[2])) / denom if denom > 0: tstart = max(tstart, tclip) else: tend = min(tend, tclip) else: if (plane.normal[0]volorigin[0] + plane.normal[1]volorigin[1] + plane.normal[2]volorigin[2]) < plane.dist: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if tstart > tend: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] t = tstart while t <= tend: pos = [volorigin[i] + t voldir[i] for i in range(3)] voxel = volumedata.sampletrilinear(pos) # Check ROI mask if maskdata is not None: maskval = maskdata.sampletrilinear(pos) if maskval <= 0.5: t += volstep continue colorval, alphaval = transferfunction(voxel) color[0] = color[0] + colorval[0] alphaval (1.0 - color[3]) color[1] = color[1] + colorval[1] alphaval (1.0 - color[3]) color[2] = color[2] + colorval[2] alphaval (1.0 - color[3]) color[3] = color[3] + alphaval (1.0 - color[3]) if color[3] >= 0.99: break t += volstep return color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Clipping boundaries must be handled carefully to avoid gaps or overlaps, especially with floating-point ray marching. Degenerate Input: If the ROI is empty or the ray does not intersect the ROI, the pixel should be transparent or background-colored. Mask Alignment: The auxiliary mask volume must be aligned with the data volume to ensure correct sample lookup. Front-to-Back Depth Peeling (FtBDP) is a technique for Region of Interest (ROI) rendering that defines an ROI as a 3D envelope by combining polygon-based depth peeling with volume ray casting. It solves the problem of visualizing internal volume features bounded by an arbitrary surface by breaking the ray casting process into stages synchronized with intermediate peeling results. Unlike standard depth peeling which only handles polygonal models, FtBDP interleaves polygon rendering and volume ray casting to correctly handle volume samples both inside and outside the envelope. A technique to attenuate unimportant high-intensity structures (e.g., at the brain surface) by defining a spherical Region of Interest (ROI) around a Point of Interest (POI) in the tumor tissue. The user marks a POI in the tumor tissue, close to the middle point. From this POI, N rays are cast: three along the coordinate system axes and three against the direction of the axes. For each ray, the distance to the POI is computed as soon as the intensity becomes less than an intensity threshold, indicating the ray has exited the suspicious structure. The maximal distance among the six rays is used to specify the radius of the spherical ROI. Only voxels inside this ROI are blended with the additional volume. Typical value: N = 6. A method to suppress unimportant structures by automatically computing a Region of Interest (ROI) from a user-marked Point of Interest (POI) using intensity analysis along cast rays. The user marks a POI, rays are cast from the POI into the volume, and intensity analysis along the cast rays computes the ROI. Time Complexity: Depends on the ROI definition. Mask-based rendering requires sampling the mask volume at each step, increasing memory bandwidth usage. Intensity-based ROI requires pre-casting rays to determine radius, adding a one-time cost. Memory Complexity: Mask-based ROI requires an auxiliary binary volume M of the same dimensions as the data volume V. Strengths: Allows precise isolation of internal structures; supports arbitrary shapes; reduces visual clutter from occluding high-intensity structures. Limitations: Geometric clipping may not fit complex internal structures; mask-based methods require pre-computation or storage of the mask; intensity-based methods depend on threshold selection. When to Use: When internal structures are occluded by high-intensity surfaces or when focusing on a specific anatomical region. When Not to Use: When the entire volume context is needed; when the ROI definition is ambiguous or difficult to specify. The technique is used in medical imaging to visualize internal pathological tissues, such as tumors, by suppressing unimportant surrounding structures. The ROI can be moved and resized by moving and rotating the wand. The technique is supported by various graphics libraries, including VTK. name: Front-to-Back Depth Peeling
head: FtBDP
body: Front-to-Back Depth Peeling (FtBDP) is a technique for Region of Interest (ROI) rendering that defines an ROI as a 3D envelope by combining polygon-based depth peeling with volume ray casting. It solves the problem of visualizing internal volume features bounded by an arbitrary surface by breaking the ray casting process into stages synchronized with intermediate peeling results. Unlike standard depth peeling which only handles polygonal models, FtBDP interleaves polygon rendering and volume ray casting to correctly handle volume samples both inside and outside the envelope. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Polygonal envelope geometry (tagged with a vertex attribute key), volume dataset, MIDA visualization settings for inside/outside regions, initial ray starting positions (optional, for optimization). Outputs: Final composited image with ROI visualization. Data Structures Depth Buffer: Stores depth values of fragments for tracking peeled surfaces. Color Buffer: Stores accumulated color from previous peeling and ray casting passes. Ray Position Buffer: Stores 3D intersection positions of rays with peeled envelope surfaces from previous steps. Envelope Geometry Tag: A vertex attribute key distinguishing envelope polygons from regular scene geometry. Numbered Steps The method proceeds in a sequence of peeling and ray casting stages: 1. Initial Peeling: Render the front-most polygonal geometry (the front surface of the envelope) normally. Store the depths of all corresponding fragments for every pixel in the depth buffer. 2. First Ray Casting Stage: Initiate MIDA ray casting. Pass the color and depth buffers from Step 1 as textures. Perform a depth test; render only volume parts that fall outside the envelope. Blend the colors from the previous peeling pass with the ray casting results. Store the positions of rays intersecting the peeled surface (from Step 1) in a separate buffer. 3. Next Peeling Stage: Initiate the next envelope peeling stage. Pass the depth results of the previous peeling pass as a texture. Choose new fragments that satisfy the depth test condition (depth > stored texture values). Store the depth values of all newly chosen fragments in the depth buffer. 4. Subsequent Ray Casting Stage: Initiate MIDA ray casting. Pass the color and depth buffers from Step 3, as well as the ray positions and accumulated color results from Step 2, as textures. Initialize ray starting positions from the stored values. Perform the depth test. Render sampled values inside or outside the envelope using different MIDA settings. Blend the colors from the previous peeling pass and the previous ray casting pass with the current ray casting results. Store the positions of rays intersecting the newly peeled surface (from Step 3) in the ray position buffer. 5. Iteration: Repeat Steps 3 and 4 until the envelope peeling stage reports 0 newly chosen fragments. Formulas Fragment selection condition: d{frag} > d{texture}, where d{frag} is the depth of a candidate fragment and d{texture} is the stored depth value from the previous peeling pass. Inside/Outside determination: A ray sample is classified as inside if it lies between a front-facing and a back-facing envelope fragment; otherwise it is outside. Parameters MIDA Settings: Visualization parameters for rendering volume samples inside vs. outside the envelope. Depth Test Condition: Comparison operator (e.g., >) to select fragments behind previously peeled surfaces. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Open Surfaces: Extreme cases where the envelope geometry crosses metaball grid boundaries and no longer forms a closed surface are handled correctly. Overdraw: The full geometry of the scene must be drawn and tested in each polygon peeling pass, leading to overdraw. Shader Overhead: There is overhead associated with shader code initialization and execution per stage. Precision and boundary handling are not specified beyond the open-surface case. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobackdepthpeeling(envelopegeometry, volumedata, insidesettings, outsidesettings): # Initialize buffers depthbuffer = [0.0] (width height) colorbuffer = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] (width height) raypositionbuffer = [None] (width height) # Step 1: Initial Peeling # Render front-most polygonal geometry (front surface of envelope) normally. # Store depths of all corresponding fragments for every pixel in the depth buffer. depthbuffer = renderfrontsurface(envelopegeometry) # Step 2: First Ray Casting Stage # Pass color and depth buffers from Step 1 as textures. # Perform depth test; render only volume parts that fall outside the envelope. # Blend previous pass colors with ray casting results. # Store ray intersection positions in a separate buffer. raycastresult2 = castvolumerays( volumedata, rayorigin=None, raydirection=None, depthtexture=depthbuffer, colortexture=colorbuffer, settings=outsidesettings, mode="outside") colorbuffer = blendbuffers(colorbuffer, raycastresult2.color) raypositionbuffer = raycastresult2.intersections # Steps 3 & 4: Iterative Peeling and Ray Casting while True: # Step 3: Next Peeling Stage # Pass depth results of previous peeling pass as a texture. # Choose new fragments satisfying the depth test condition (depth > stored texture values). # Store new fragment depths in the depth buffer. newfragments = selectfragments(envelopegeometry, depthbuffer, condition="depth > texture") if not newfragments: break depthbuffer = updatedepthbuffer(depthbuffer, newfragments) # Step 4: Subsequent Ray Casting Stage # Pass color and depth buffers from Step 3, and ray positions/accumulated colors from Step 2 as textures. # Initialize ray starting positions from stored values. # Perform depth test. Render sampled values inside/outside envelope using different MIDA settings. # Blend previous peeling and ray casting results with current results. # Store new ray intersection positions. raycastresult4 = castvolumerays( volumedata, rayorigin=raypositionbuffer, raydirection=None, depthtexture=depthbuffer, colortexture=colorbuffer, settingsinside=insidesettings, settingsoutside=outsidesettings) colorbuffer = blendbuffers(colorbuffer, raycastresult4.color) raypositionbuffer = raycastresult4.intersections return colorbuffer Time Complexity: The method involves multiple passes. Each peeling pass requires drawing the full geometry and performing depth tests. Each ray casting pass involves volume sampling and blending. The number of passes depends on the complexity of the envelope depth layers. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for depth buffers, color buffers, and ray position buffers. Performance: No additional GPU computational workload for ray casting is introduced by keeping and initializing ray positions between stages. However, overhead exists from shader initialization/execution per stage and overdraw from the depth peeling algorithm. Strengths: Allows for complex ROI definitions using implicit surfaces (metaballs) and handles open envelope surfaces. Correctly blends polygonal and volumetric data. Limitations: Overdraw and shader overhead can impact performance. Requires careful management of buffer passing between passes. Front-to-Back Depth Peeling was introduced in the context of a 3D painting metaphor for volume image exploration. It extends the concept of depth peeling, which traditionally deals only with polygonal models, to integrate with volume ray casting. The technique was developed to support an envelope definition using GPU-accelerated metaballs, allowing for growing and editing of the ROI in a manner similar to placing brush strokes. The term "Front-to-Back" refers to the order of peeling, which matches the front-to-back order of ray casting.
